东海道新干线当初建设的目的是作为「东海道本线的轨道增加」，从这个点来说的话，除了支线以外全线都是「双复线」以上。但是在JR路线的名称公告里，东海道新干线及山阳新干线（新大阪站－新神户站）都是当做为没有东海道本线名称的「支线」（在1982年东北新干线开业以前都是单纯增加轨道）。另一方面，基本事业计划与国土交通省监修的《铁道要览》是当作别的路线。

概要
包含了日本最早开通的铁道：新桥站（后为汐留货物站（），现已不存）－横滨站（现在的樱木町站）间，沿著东海道（严格说来包含一部份的美浓路、中山道）连结东京至神户的沿线都市。

有经营定期旅客业务的支线包含大垣站－美浓赤坂站间（通称「美浓赤坂线」）、大垣站－（新垂井）－关原站间（下行线是为了勾配缓和的别线，现在下行优等列车为通过状态）以及作为横须贺线运转的品川站－新川崎站－鹤见站间（通称：品鹤线）。首都圈、名古屋近郊、京阪神地区另有许多货物支线（如东海道货运线等）。

在东京近郊与京阪神地区中，电车线是并行行驶的（东京站－品川站间的山手线、东京站－横滨站间的京滨东北线、京都站－西明石站间的东海道、山阳线普通电车都是属于东海道本线电车线）。在东京近郊的列车线中，设有快速列车线的位置。在京阪神地区中新快速与一部份快速使用的列车线，以及大部分的快速与普通使用的电车线，在原则上是采用混合行驶的运用方式。在东京站－小田原站及草津站－神户站（实际上为山阳本线西明石站）之间的一部分区间为双复线或以上的轨道配置，而部分并行的货物线，东海道、山阳本线各站停车的普通电车线，及山手线、京滨东北线、横须贺线等其他路线则是分别平行设置。

在JR西日本管辖内米原站－神户站之间，通常会赋予区间路线暱称。其中米原站－京都站间为琵琶湖线的一部份、京都站－大阪站间是JR京都线、大阪站－神户站间则是JR神户线的一部份。由JR西日本运营的山阳新干线在到达新大阪站时，车内播送的换车资讯会使用上述暱称，但由JR东海运营的东海道新干线侧则会使用正式名称「东海道线」。

东京站－热海站间包含东京近郊区间，米原站－神户站间包含大阪近郊区间，东京近郊区间是东京站－大船站间、品川站－新川崎站－鹤见站间，大阪近郊区间的京都站－神户站间包含电车特定区间。

2001年9月21日开始在东京近郊区间，湘南新宿线快速列车经由新宿站往高崎线的直通列车运转开始。自蛇洼信号场至户冢站间于横须贺线的电车路线上行驶。

此外，在2015年3月14日因东北、上越新干线建设而一度废止之东北本线列车线由上野站延伸至东京站，宇都宫线、高崎线、常磐线的各线开始直通运行（上野东京线）。

全区间是代表日本的动脉，在西边的终点神户站则和山阳本线连接在一起。除了夜行列车以外，远距离的旅客输送已经让给了东海道新干线，运行通过全区间的大多是货物列车。除了关原以外的地区都全年温暖，为了改良坡道也做了缓和，事实上「平坦线、暖地向」、「干线机」等形式，多半是以本线为基准开发的车辆。（如国铁113系电车、国铁C59型蒸气机关车、国铁C62型蒸气机关车、国铁EF57型电气机关车、国铁EH10型电气机关车、国铁EF65型电气机关车、国铁EF66型电气机关车、JR货物EF200型电气机关车等）。

名称
单独称呼东海道线（）时，不仅仅是指旧『日本国有铁道线路名称』的东海道本线以及其支线，还包含了山手线、横须贺线、御殿场线、身延线、饭田线、武丰线、福知山线等及其支线，现在都是简称为东海道本线。

在东海道本线运行的列车全线都使用东海道线来作称呼。在东京近郊东京站－热海站间的中距离电车旅客简介都使用这个名称（车站、车内的广播、行先表示），JR东海于东海道本线管辖内的全部区间，也就是沼津、静冈、名古屋、岐阜周边都使用「东海道线」来做介绍。米原以西的JR西日本区间也有称呼「东海道线」的情形，但在1988年3月该公司决定琵琶湖线、JR京都线、JR神户线等暱称后，多半都是使用这些暱称。

在传播媒体中，近畿的地方电视新闻、神户新闻与京都新闻、地方裁判所的土地公示广告、都市再生机构与民间不动产公司的广告、一部份的地图集（包含汽车导航、网路地图）一般都使用琵琶湖线、（JR）京都线、（JR）神户线，全国版的新闻节目与报纸除朝日新闻、朝日放送（ABC）以外，原则上皆使用东海道（本）线。

沿线风景
虽然有著东海道的名称，但是多半不是走在海岸线上，能够看到海景的路段仅限于平冢、国府津－热海、三岛、由比、滨名湖、蒲郡周围。原来东海道这个名称由来是因为沿著是江户时代五街道中的旧东海道舖设而来，是将古代律令时代制定之五畿七道，即东海、南关东等所指地域（三重、爱知、静冈、山梨、神奈川、千叶、茨城等）连结而成的街道，并非单指海岸沿线的区域。

当初铺设时距离海岸线有一点距离，有一说是军部担心外国舰队可能会利用舰砲射击铁道，实际上当初明治政府原本决定要沿著中山道铺设干线，但因在山岳地带铺设有困难，因此改为东海道路线，之后的山阳铁道（山阳本线）选择离海岸有一点距离铺设就是来自军部的要求。之后于滨名湖北侧迂回的二俣线（现在的天龙滨名湖铁道），是为了避免湖与太平洋的连结而建，于1940年（昭和15年）通车。

比较有力的说法是以当时的土木技术与车辆性能来说，因为隧道与坡度的限制，舖设条件相当有限，东海道海岸沿线有许多地方地形险恶，因此选择以内陆路线迂回，地形不佳的旧东海道丰桥－冈崎与铃鹿峠改以其他路线，京都－大阪以京街道对岸行驶，国府津－沼津、关原周边、山科周边在编成扩大以后，以坡度较小的路线替代。

品川与横滨附近以靠近海岸线的路线铺设，因为用地无法取得，品川站是盖在填海地中，在横滨之前的路段是在浅海中填土做成的，这些地方因为是填海地的关系，都再也看不到海。

JR东日本辖下路段
东海道本线的起点站东京站，是集中JR各线、国内少数的大型终点站。东海道线列车由东京站离开后，在品川站之前是与山手线、京滨东北线、东海道新干线并行，也与同路段的地下路线横须贺线以及都营地下铁浅草线－京急本线并行。在东京－小田原间，主要都是在办公街、繁华商业街、住宅街中行驶，川崎站－横滨站间是在工厂、仓库以及中继货物设施中通过，在保土谷－东户冢间，贯穿三浦半岛延续而来的棱线之隧道（清水谷户隧道），是日本现役铁道隧道中最早兴建的。大矶－国府津间则变成田园景色，其他地区则有著广大的关东近郊沿线风景。横滨站附近的列车原本是沿著海岸行驶，现在的横滨站是建立在填海地上，该站的东口是广大的购物街，已经不再能够感受到多少海的气息。在崇光百货横滨Sogo（Sogo横滨店）东侧的横滨BAY QUARTER2楼，连结著的栈桥是往港未来21（）、红砖仓库、山下码头（冰川丸前）的开船之处。在平冢站前之相模川桥梁上可以从车窗远眺相模湾。在小田原站－真鹤站间，因为山与海直接相连，所以是隧道较多的路段，在隧道与隧道之间可以反复的看到蜜柑田与相模湾蓝色的海景。靠近根府川站的白糸川铁桥是有名的摄影地点，在好天气时可以看到西北侧箱根山的外轮山。以前的根府川站因关东大地震造成的土石灾害崩落沈入海中，现在海底还残存当时的月台。真鹤站是最靠近因相模湾而生产丰盛海产之真鹤渔港的车站，周边有许多具有新鲜鱼贝类的饮食店。汤河原站之前是小田原以西最初的广大平地，这里的山脚有因梅园而有名的幕山公园。汤河原是著名作家或政治家最常隐居的汤河原温泉之玄关，特别是在夏天有许多往吉滨海水浴场的旅客。离开汤河原跨过流著汤河原温泉的千岁川后便进入静冈县，经过泉越隧道越过伊豆山，便到达日本少数温泉都市也是与JR东海辖下路段交界车站热海。

热海－丰桥
在热海站之东南侧太平洋海岸（相模滩）有温泉街，车站与温泉街之间的土产物店林立。离开热海后可以看见伊东线的来宫站，与其并行的东海道线在此并无月台，只有电留线。不久之后西侧是丹那隧道的入口，丹那隧道的钻掘工事是有著许多死伤者的困难工事。离开丹那隧道通过函南与山地后到达三岛，三岛是一个充满富士泉水之清流的地方，也是通往修善寺温泉、天城汤岛温泉的西侧玄关口，于清流中孕育而生的鳗鱼料理是值得期待的绝品。此后，沼津是渔港的市镇，在沼津港鱼市场旁，有许多可以享用骏河湾鱼产油炸品的饮食店，此处也是西伊豆观光的窗口，2016年开始因动漫Love Live! Sunshine!!以沼津为场景，吸引动漫迷造访，成为圣地巡礼点。在吉原－富士川之间，如果天气好的话，可以眺望到雄壮的富士山。通过曾在山部赤人诗歌中登场过的田子之浦后，便到达以造纸工厂闻名的吉原、富士。富士市与吉原市（现今富士市）过去曾充满著造纸工厂的废气，但是近年来在造纸公司的努力下已经有大幅的改善。

渡过富士川往静冈市方向，在蒲原－清水间，于山崖与海之间的狭窄平坦地行驶，海侧与国道1号、东名高速道路并行，经过由比站后，面海的视线被高速道路所遮蔽。在由比站附近是曾以由比渔港炸正樱虾、日本𫚖为题材的观光地，东海道广重美术馆位于车站出来沿旧东海道步行约15－20分的地方，沿著此一道路上散在有以正樱虾为中心的海鲜贩卖店、饮食店。在清水站里因线路为南北向的缘故，可以在海侧车窗看到富士山，此站是最靠近代表足球王国静冈的日本职业足球联赛（J联盟）球队清水心跳之母球场静冈市清水日本平运动公园球技场、日本三大松原之一—三保。次一站草薙站是最靠近草薙神社的车站，也是静冈县相关设施（静冈县立大学、静冈县立美术馆、静冈县立图书馆、县草薙总合运动场）的入口站，距离静冈铁道草薙站徒步只要三分钟。东静冈站是为了货物操车场旧址再开发商业地区而设置的车站，今后静冈市行政厅舍预计将移转至此地，也是名胜日本平、久能山东照宫与静冈大学的入口站，以塑胶模型等产品世界闻名的模型公司田宫模型（TAMIYA）也在本站南方。离开东静冈后，可以看到北侧静冈车辆区以及办公大楼街道的高架车站，就是静冈县县都、政令指定都市静冈市的中心车站—静冈站。静冈站是高架车站，南侧是东海道新干线的月台，同站北口是静铁以及JR东海巴士的终点站，从此处到市内各处、县内以及县外各地几乎全部的巴士路线都由此发车，地方主要交通工具静冈铁道之新静冈站位于本站北侧徒步7－8分的位置上，此处北侧的骏府城内有静冈县厅，堀外西侧是静冈市役所静冈厅舍、葵区役所，以静冈厅舍、葵区役所为中心有两替町、吴服町等广大的繁华街。离开静冈后，直接渡过安倍川，安倍川年糕是静冈有名的土产，在旧东海道安西桥（现为安倍川桥，从与东海道本线并行的国道1号上架设的骏河大桥之一，上游处可以见到的旧国道1号上架设之桥梁）的「府中宿」旁之老舗「石部屋（）」，依旧可以品尝到传统的味道，此桥对岸的山间有以「山药泥与麦饭」闻名的东海道「丸子宿（）」，这附近与神奈川县汤河原－静冈县磐田附近相同，在较低之山的缓斜面，几乎都是茶田与蜜柑田。通过安倍川、用宗再经过长隧道后，便到达烧津。此路段的海岸线，有连续陡峭断崖的知名胜景，被称为「东海的亲不知」之「大崩海岸」亦在此处。原本东海道线是利用隧道沿著此处海岸铺设，但是因为海浪侵蚀海岸的状况很严重，因此沿用先前失败的弹丸列车计划而完成日本坂隧道路线，此后因台风使护岸与旧隧道坑口崩坏，在海岸上仍有残骸留存。之后此一日本坂隧道又因新干线建设的需要不得不让出，因此再度利用一度放弃的石部、矶滨这两个旧隧道，避开崩坏的旧坑口，在内部建立隧道联系使用。旧东海道与国道1号避开此一海岸线，于山间迂回越过宇津之谷峠。自西烧津至岛田间行驶于开阔的平地，在以行驶蒸气机车而知名的大井川铁道之起点金谷前，渡过被称呼为「」的大井川。在金谷与菊川间行驶于产茶地「牧之原台地」的山缝间，通过袋井附近后进入平地，渡过天龙川进入「乐器之町」滨松。在舞阪－新居町间渡过滨名湖时可以在左右两侧见到湖水，其中辩天岛站位于滨名湖中的岛上。这里是过去东海道新干线开业前，于东京站与大阪站同时间发车的在来线特急「」号会车的地方。离开滨名湖不多久便进入爱知县，到达东三河地区的中核都市丰桥。

丰桥－米原
进入爱知县后仍然是广大的平原。离开丰桥后，有机会看见名古屋铁道及饭田线的列车。在蒲郡市内可能看到三河湾及渥美半岛，之后往西的方向不会再沿著海岸线前进，沿线是住宅地及田园地带。离开冈崎站后，从冈崎市中心转左，通过矢作川。之后向直前进，经过安城站及刈谷站。经过刈谷站跳过三大都市圈的工业区及住宅地中行驶。离开大府站后进入名古屋市区。在大高站至笠寺站附近与东海道新干线使用同一条路线。于热田站附近与名铁多条行车线并行，在东海地方以及东海道本线仍使用手动式平交道。离开名古屋市南方中端站金山站后，是与新干线及中央本线同时行走的路线。在名古屋站四周有很多摩天大厦及名古屋高速道路，而到达拥有日本最高层的车站大厦名古屋站。

列车自名古屋站出发后，一旁可看到由地下延伸出来的名铁名古屋本线。之后便与名铁名古屋本线分离，跨越庄内川而离开名古屋市区。从右方可看到东海道货物根据车站稻泽站，左方是尾张一宫站。之后与名铁线在同一线道行驶，并穿越木曾川。在木曾川铁桥上C62型蒸气火车曾以每小时129公里作高速测试。

列车再度在高架路线上行驶，然后就左转到达岐阜站。岐阜是一个观光城市，曾是斋藤道三及织田信长居城，岐阜城（稻叶山城）及长良川。可以从高架桥观赏岐阜地区及金华山的景色。

岐阜与大垣之间经过长良川及揖斐川，在浓尾平野上大致以直线通过。

大垣在以前是越过关原的辅助机车的基地，直到现在电力动车组普及的年代，这个基地仍是附近列车的基地对列车服务作出不少贡献。可以看到大垣电车区，经过南荒尾信号场。之后是前往美浓赤坂支线的分叉线，可以看到支线上的荒尾站。向美浓赤坂的电车在荒尾经过，以低速横过工厂到达美浓赤坂站。美浓赤坂站是货物线西浓铁道的延伸。

南荒尾信号场是山麓下山线道通称为垂井线。从大垣至关原之间为连续的陡坡路段，因此在战争期间为增强运输能力而设置别线，让特急列车及货物列车使用。在此路段的新垂井站，因下行线的列车不会停站而有名，1986年车站被停止使用。垂井站停车是普通电车由旧下行线前进，特急及货物列车从山麓之下行驶。再向前一点就是关原站。

从此至醒井间可看到伊吹山。越过关原后，是东海道本线之中路况最坏的路段，这里是暴雪地区之一。此外，大垣至米原之间是县境边界，是连接东海与关西两大日本经济领域的地区，当地交通流动量较少，因此列车的车卡较少。

通过伊吹山背后即进入近江盆地的田园地带，到达JR西日本营运地区的边境车站米原站。

米原－京都
可以转乘新干线以及往敦贺方向之北陆本线的米原站，过去是属于名古屋铁道管理局管辖，国铁分割民营化后移转为JR西日本所属，位于车站北侧由过去机关区旧址改成的电留线相当广阔，也可以见到于南侧货物列车用发著线与操车场旧址所新设之JR总研的大型风洞设施。

自米原起的路段被称之为琵琶湖线。过去行驶于米原－彦根间湖岸（松原内湖），现在内湖已经被填平，故不能看到琵琶湖。米原－膳所之间是东海道线最后的开通的路段，1889年（明治22年）开通后，开始行驶东海道线直通列车，因行驶湖东平原的平坦地，是曲线很少的路段。边望著过去井伊家的居城彦根城进入彦根站，这里过去是以近江铁道为媒介，转运水泥与啤酒的地方。以桥梁来回通过宇曾川、爱知川，通过较小的腰越山隧道右手边是做为织田信长居城闻名的安土山（安土城址）。

近江八幡站是接续往八日市的近江铁道之据点。车站周围有许多住宅，因此通勤通学乘客相当多，此外也是乐中以船巡游近江商人街等休闲活动之著名地点。

在田园地带里可以看到电车车库的是野洲站，从此站开始进入京都、大阪通勤圈，因此在田园地带中住宅逐渐增加，以野洲起始往大阪方向的电车也很多，之后的守山、栗东在车站前可以看到住宅大厦群。之后是连结草津线的草津站，在琵琶湖线内是利用旅客较多且热闹的车站。

自草津开始行驶于1970年完成的四线路段。渡过可以见到琵琶湖湖面的濑田川桥梁，之后是石山站，本站与之后的膳所站都可以转乘京阪电铁石山坂本线，膳所过去一度被称为大津站，此处过去设有机关区。依逢坂山的路线处于较高的位置自车窗可以望见琵琶湖。

称之为大津的车站过去曾经多次改换位置，现在的大津站是第三代，是改换为经过1921年完成的新逢坂山、东山隧道的目前路线后，所新设的车站。车站的西侧便是新逢坂山隧道，通过隧道可以看见头上高架的湖西线。由车窗内还分不清楚府县境，便进入京都府的山科站，在山科站可以转乘湖西线，并联络京阪电铁京津线、京都市营地下铁东西线的终点站。由山科起进入大的土堤，穿越东山隧道，渡过鸭川便到达京都站。

京都－尼崎
京都站是拥有0号线－34号线（没有15－29号，实际共20线）的月台编号，一个大型的终点站。不仅仅是京都观光与通往京阪神的通勤输送据点，也是关西空港直通特急及往北近畿、北陆、山阴各观光地特急起点的观光据点站。于1997年完成具未来感全玻璃外墙的新大楼具有大终点站存在感的威容，车站周边持续进行新大楼的开发。京都站是全部新干线列车的停车站，嵯峨野线与奈良线、私铁的近铁京都线、京都市营地下铁也有驶入本站。

由京都发车不久之后便会在右手侧看到广大的路线群，距离列车较近的是梅小路货运站，较远的是梅小路蒸气火车博物馆。梅小路蒸气机关车馆是以昔日属于东海道线、山阴线蒸气机关车一大基地的梅小路机关区为母体，现地保存蒸气机关车的地方，如果时间上凑巧的话，可以在东海道线的车窗看见蒸气机关车的所冒出的烟。

渡过桂川，通过向日町站后，在左侧可以看到一个很大的车辆基地，这是京都总合运转所，以前的向日町运转所，自开设当时起成为山阳、山阴、北陆各线的优等列车基地，虽然较过去减少很多班次，但还是能在白天看到寝台列车休息的姿态。

通过名神高速道路的大型红色铁桥后与阪急电铁京都线接近并行，过去超特急燕与阪急京都线之前身新京阪线电车之相互竞走是相当有名的画面。之后行驶于突出淀川之天王山山麓，中途到达山崎站，此一车站的月台有京都、大阪之府境标示。

山崎自古以来便是京都以及大阪间的交通要道，为天王山与男山中间夹著淀川的狭小地形，当中仅有的平地便夹有东海道线、阪急京都线、东海道新干线、西国街道以及与淀川斜交之京街道、京阪本线等。因为是明智光秀军队被羽柴秀吉打败之古战场而知名。车站周边的曲线是东海道本线以及关西地区最佳之列车摄影地，在铁道爱好者间相当有名。

通过山崎的隘口，快速行驶于广阔的平原，列车经过成为大阪住宅区之高槻、茨木后进入千里丘。从这里开始到吹田，车窗的右侧是荒凉的吹田调车场旧址，左侧是JR货物的吹田机务段以及JR西日本吹田工场，千里丘附近还有阪急电铁正雀工场与ALNA工机，因此也可见到阪急的车辆。

在吹田的南侧，跨过阪急千里线，分歧出连结片町线鴫野的城东货物线，渡过神崎川之后进入淀川区，便到达东淀川站，战前的弹丸列车计划中原本预定于东淀川设立新线的车站，但最后新干线的设计是在东淀川以南连接新车站，东淀川站与下站新大阪站的距离只有短短的700m，在这短短的700m之间的平交道有8线轨道穿越，被称为打不开的平交道而闻名。

新大阪站是东海道本线及新干线的转运站，设有前往山阴、和歌山、长野的特急及大阪市营地下铁路线的车站。以新大阪为起点，正在建设纵贯大阪东部的大阪外环状线。新大阪站在刚通车不久所看到的四周都是田园风景，现在成为大阪的商业街。

然后穿越淀川，可从左边看到HEP Nabio的红色大观览车，大阪市北部的中心，到达大阪市梅田大阪站，这个车站名称各公社有所差异，是阪神、阪急、大阪市营地下铁各公司的总站。现在在大阪站外又再度开发及进行车站改善工程。

京阪间的地区在战前是阪急、京阪之间的竞争非常激烈，过往至今是京阪的路线与阪急京都线，现在为了作商业竞争会看到列车一起并排行走。JR京都线是与阪急、京阪，JR神户线是与阪急、阪神及从京都至东海道本线终点前的私营铁路的竞争。JR投入新快速的服务，完结速度之间的竞争，现今改为服务方面的竞争。由于与私铁价钱的竞争，京阪神的东海道本线路段以特价车票吸引顾客，可以在使用平日黄昏，星期六日间使用特价车票（请参见都市网路（）条目）。

经过大阪站再度穿越-{淀}-川，经过冢本站后穿越神崎川进入兵库县。

尼崎－神户
进入尼崎站后，即进入兵库县一带。尼崎站是福知山线（JR宝冢线）、JR东西线转换到新快速及福知山线（JR宝冢线）的特急列车在此停靠。这里开始是芦屋周围，再次于市中心及住宅区之间行驶。离开尼崎站的下一站是立花站。立花站是最接近尼崎市役所的车站。最多乘客于此站停留。下一个车站是甲子园口站，与甲子园球场的阪神电铁甲子园站相距达2公里。此外，JR神户线与终点站为大阪梅田的阪急神户线、阪神本线的线路相当接近，进入三家竞争。从北顺序排列是阪急神户线、JR神户线及阪神本线。

离开甲子园口后进入西宫站。阪急电车的大型转乘站西宫北口站都在西宫市。列车在住宅区中快速行驶，之后到达芦屋站。芦屋地区是战前关西超高级住宅区而闻名，在车站外再多走一步可看到住宅并排。西之宫以西是1995年阪神淡路大地震受到大规模破坏的地区。

芦屋－三之宫－神户之间的北方是以天然水及远足有名的六甲山。海拔高度为900米，山景与铁路紧迫，身体若伸出窗外会有危险。芦屋川与六甲线路车接连住吉站。这是学校车站是离滩高等学校最接近车站。离开芦屋，到达地震严重破坏后重建的六甲道站及滩站、列车在兵库神户地区市中心的三之宫站、元町站停留。

三之宫站是阪急、阪神电车的中央车站，车站间隔相当接近。就因为这样，由大阪至这里是JR神户线人流最多的地区。神户高速铁道、港之线、神户市营地下铁终端车站，在元町、三宫地区铁道中心站以外有与世界联系的神户港、神户空港。沿海有神户Broad Tower、神户海洋博物馆，亦可看到海景。街北方是异人馆，以前是外国人居留地区。元町站高架下的元町高架下商店街有不少外国船员，另外华侨聚居的南京町，是与横滨及长崎并列为日本三大唐人街。

经过元町后，是东海道本线终点车站神户站。神户站是神户地区的中央车站。而主要转运站则让给三之宫站。此外亦是离神户哈勃兰德、神户光之祭会场最接近的车站，新快速列车亦会停车。此上连接山阳新干线的是新神户站，而不是神户站，可在三之宫站之前转乘神户市营地下铁西神、山手线前往。

由京都方向前往西明石站及姬路站为止的列车为多为直通运行，而在神户站以西开始的车站是属于山阳本线，东海道本线就此结束。

运行方式
在东海道新干线开业之后，主要都倾向于重视地区运送，全线通行运转的列车多半是夜行列车。列车运转的现况见以下叙述。

地区输送
全线行驶通过东海道腰带地带，在各地区设有频繁运行的地区列车，特别是东京站－热海站、滨松站－大垣站、米原站－神户站－姬路站（※神户站－姬路站间属山阳本线）。各区间是涵盖东京、名古屋、大阪等大都市圈的各公司重点路线之所在（东京站－热海站是湘南电车、经过新宿直通高崎线列车是湘南新宿线、米原站－京都站是琵琶湖线、京都站－大阪站是JR京都线、大阪站－神户站是JR神户线，请参阅各线之条目）。

在这之中，静冈地区与名古屋地区等区域，没有进行双复线化的近郊区间专用线建设以便分离旅客与货物，长年都以货物列车与长距离列车优先，造成地区输送列车运行上很大的制约。但是从1980年代以后，随著铁道货物运送的减少，使近距离旅客列车得以大量增加班次。

现在，在这些区间内实施著高频率的地区运送。静冈地区内的快速列车有平日早晚在三岛－滨松间运转的「Home Liner（）」、夜行快速「月光长良（）」。一部份的列车没有厕所（113系、115系中的一部份、211系5000、6000番台全部编成），接续的形式在热海站－丰桥站间也有全部没有厕所的情形，地方的顾客有很多抱怨，因此，JR东海在2007年春季以前将没有厕所的113系编成，在静冈地区计划导入各编成皆有厕所的313系。

京都站－神户站间有阪急电铁、京阪电气铁道、阪神电气铁道等强力的竞争者，为了与其对抗，运行以具有高速运转与容易了解的时刻表等特点之新快速（可直通至一部分北陆本线、湖西线、山阳本线），在2005年JR福知山线脱轨事故发生以来，开始由重视速度朝向重视安全性方向调整。

在以名古屋站为中心的中部地方中有开行新快速与特别快速。新快速在丰桥－滨松间与岐阜－米原间是各站停车，名古屋－滨松间约105km的区间以1小时15－20分连结，冈崎－丰桥间的快速、新快速通过站在日间以普通列车每30分钟的间隔运行。

东京圈－北关东间的铁道需求
2000年、日本运输省（现国土交通省）针对全国各都道府县，进行该年度都道府县间铁道流动量的调查。在关东地方的调查结果中可以得知，在现在湘南新宿线行走区间中东京圈－北关东间的铁道需求非常高。因为此背景因素，2002年湘南新宿线开业。此外，当局决定兴建东北纵贯线，并于2015年以上野东京线名义通车，令现时乘客可以乘搭东海道线列车直接前往上野站以北地方。

历史
东海道本线延伸的历史可以说是象征著日本初期铁道的历史。

最早的路段是在新桥－横滨间以及神户－京都间，象征著都市的文化，之后开始有兴建连结关东与关西的计划产生。由当初预定的中山道路径变更为东海道路径后，成为一个庞大的计划，建设速度大幅进展。

但在当时，神户站－大津站间以及长滨站－关原站－大府站－武丰站间，为了要输送建设资材而建设的铁道逐渐开业，为了要连结名阪神，大津与长滨间开设了日本最早的火车渡轮－太湖汽船，因此在将既有路线积极活用以便降低建设预算的前提下，东海道本线名古屋－草津之间并非江户时代的东海道，改沿著美浓路与中山道路径铺设。此外当时，在东海道本线路线之外，关西铁道于热田（名古屋）－龟山－草津之间，以振兴沿线经济为目的铺设铁道，也就是现在的草津线与关西本线。

开始之初，因为「宿场的客人不会再来」「火车会造成火灾」等等来自宿场的反对理由，无法取得市街用地因此多半选择建设于郊外的路径，因此车站设置地点多半距离宿场较远。大众认知到铁路的便利性后，街道的机能便逐渐转移至车站附近，连结车站与旧街道间的铁道也就大量的开始兴建。

兴建时因为沿岸伊豆、箱根、伊吹山、逢坂山等地方需要挖掘隧道，难度较高，因此采用较内陆的走线（山线）。其后于1920年代兴建海线部分，该路段于1934年开通后，取代山线成为本线，而原来山线路段则成为现在的御殿场线。

对台湾铁路建设贡献极大的长谷川谨介曾在1878年至1889年参与东海道本线的建设，并将他在建设东海道线时培育出的优秀技术及管理能力带到台湾。

2001年开始，经由新宿站与高崎线直通运转（湘南新宿线）。

在2015年，JR东日本把列车线透过上野东京线把东北本线连接起来，列车可经由东京站与宇都宫线、高崎线、常磐线等开始相互直通运行，东海道线的列车从此跟东北本线的列车直通运行，令东海道线列车运行范围扩大。

章节.Late Shōwa and Early Heisei Periods:
On October 1, 1964 (Showa 39), the Tokaido Shinkansen between Tokyo Station and Shin-Osaka Station opened. At the time, the fastest service, the "Hikari," initially took 4 hours to travel between the two stations, and from the following year onward, it operated in 3 hours and 10 minutes. As the Shinkansen became the mainstay of transportation between Tokyo and the Keihanshin area, the Tokaido Main Line, which had previously been called the conventional line, saw the discontinuation of many daytime limited express services and instead transformed into a route primarily focused on regional transportation. From the 1970s onward, the New Rapid service was introduced as an intercity express train to compete with parallel lines operated by other companies in the Keihanshin area. Similarly, rapid train services began to appear in the Nagoya area, operated by electric trains. In the Tokyo metropolitan area, as part of the "Five-Direction Commuting Plan," the separation of tracks for the Shonan Electric Line and the Yokosuka Line Electric Train service was carried out in 1980 (Showa 55). Since 1984 (Showa 59), in the Shizuoka and Nagoya areas, where train frequencies were low, short-distance services have been increased and scheduled at regular intervals.

On April 1, 1987 (Showa 62), following the division and privatization of Japan National Railways, the Tokaido Main Line was divided among three passenger companies and one freight company. Each company implemented transportation improvements tailored to its regional circumstances. In the Tokyo metropolitan area of JR East, where commuter rush hours are particularly severe, train capacity was increased to alleviate congestion. In the Nagoya area of JR Central and the Keihanshin area of JR West, rapid train services were increased and sped up to compete with other companies. Commuter-oriented "Commuter Liner" services also appeared successively in various regions. Airport access express services were introduced, and from 1997 (Heisei 9), through-services began on the Keihanshin slow-line electric trains via the JR West Line and the Takarazuka Line. In 2001 (Heisei 13), the Shonan-Shinjuku Line opened, and other new operating patterns emerged. JR Freight worked to increase the speed of its freight trains, and in 2004 (Heisei 16), it began operating the "Super Rail Cargo," a distributed-power freight electric train.
章节.From the Late Heisei Era Onward:
Since the late Heisei era, the Mo-Kei-Han-Shin area has undergone DC electrification south of Tsuruga Station on the Hokuriku Main Line. In the Tokyo metropolitan area, through services on this line have expanded due to the Ueno-Tokyo Line and other projects. As a result, fares for Green Cars on ordinary trains have decreased, and new features such as the A-Seat system with additional charges for the New Rapid service in the Mo-Kei-Han-Shin area have been introduced, bringing about changes to seating services. On the other hand, the aforementioned commuter liners were converted into limited express trains simultaneously with vehicle replacements, leading to the discontinuation of some trains. Except for the Shizuoka area, these services have steadily been reduced.

Night trains have seen a decline in ridership due to competition from domestic air travel and express buses. By 2009 (Heisei 21), all Blue Trains departing from and arriving at Tokyo Station had disappeared. The "Ogaki Night Train," which connected Tokyo Station and Ogaki Station as an ordinary night train, had operated since 1996 (Heisei 9) as the reserved-seat Rapid service "Moonlight Nagara." However, it became a temporary train after 2009 and ran its final service in the spring of 2020 (Reiwa 2). Since then, the only regularly scheduled night train remaining on this line—and indeed on the entire JR network—is the one round trip of the electric limited express "Sunrise Seto/Izumo." Meanwhile, new luxury sleeper trains, such as JR East's "TRAIN SUITE Shiki-shima" and JR West's "TWILIGHT EXPRESS Mizuho," have been introduced. These, also known as cruise trains, include routes within the respective companies' areas along this line.

In terms of station facilities, the introduction of Suica in 2001 (Heisei 13) marked the beginning of a broad expansion of IC card compatibility. Additionally, station numbering systems, primarily designed with foreign travelers in mind, have been implemented across all company-operated areas, with the entire Tokaido Main Line—excluding the Mino-Akasaka Branch—being fully compatible by 2021 (Reiwa 3). Efforts are also underway to install home-door systems, particularly at busy stations in major metropolitan areas.
章节.Overview:
The Tokaido Main Line, starting from Tokyo and passing through Yokohama, Shizuoka, Hamamatsu, Nagoya, Kyoto, Osaka, etc., connects to Kobe via the Pacific Belt, covering a total length of 589.5 km (excluding branch lines). Excluding its branch lines, it is the second-longest railway line in Japan, following the San'in Main Line.

On this route, the section between Shimbashi Station (later Shiodome Freight Station, now discontinued) and Yokohama Station opened in 1872 (Meiji 5) as Japan's first railway. Subsequently, in 1874 (Meiji 7), the section between Osaka Station and Kobe Station opened, and after several route extensions, the entire line between Shimbashi Station and Kobe Station opened in July 1889 (Meiji 22), connecting the Tokyo metropolitan area with the Keihanshin region by rail. Afterward, through events such as the opening of Tokyo Station and route changes in mountainous areas, the present-day Tokaido Main Line was formed. Although it was once a single line operated by Japan National Railways (JNR), following the JNR privatization and division in April 1987 (Showa 62), it was divided among three companies: JR East, JR Central, and JR West. These three passenger companies became Type 1 railway operators, owning the tracks and operating passenger trains, while JR Freight became a Type 2 railway operator, using the tracks of the three passenger companies to operate freight trains.

Since the entire line opened, it served as a major transportation artery representing Japan, connecting Tokyo with the Keihanshin (Kansai) area, the Chugoku region, and Kyushu, with numerous long-distance passenger trains operating. However, in October 1964 (Showa 39), the Tokaido Shinkansen opened with the aim of increasing transport capacity. Subsequently, the role of long-distance passenger transport was transferred to this Shinkansen, and passenger transport on the parallel Tokaido Main Line shifted to a system focused on regional transport. As of 2022, the only regular passenger trains running on the entire line are the sleeper limited express "Sunrise Seto" and "Sunrise Izumo." Between Mishima Station and Fuji Station, and between Shizuoka Station and Nagoya Station (these sections are operated by JR Tokai), no limited express trains operate except for the sleeper limited expresses. On the other hand, regarding freight transport, it continues to maintain its position as a vital artery, with numerous freight trains operated by JR Freight running. Additionally, some freight trains operate directly through the Sanyo Main Line and the Tohoku Main Line. The climate is generally warm throughout the year, except for the vicinity of Sekihara, and gradients have been mitigated through improvements.

It is rare.
The name of the line is such that it was constructed along the Tokaido route connecting Edo and Kyoto. However, between Atsuta Station and Kusatsu Station, because the line was originally planned to follow the Nakasendo, it runs along the Minoji, which is the medieval Tokaido route. Nowadays, it runs parallel to the Tokaido Main Line and serves as a major road, connecting the three major metropolitan areas of Tokyo, Nagoya, and Osaka via expressways such as the Tomei, Shin-Tomei, Meishin, and Shin-Meishin, as well as National Route 1. Nevertheless, the route differs significantly in some sections.

During the JNR era, in the “Japan National Railways Line Names,” the name “Tokaido Main Line” was used to refer to this line. The name “Tokaido Line” was used as a general term to include not only the Tokaido Main Line itself but also its branch lines, such as the Yamanote Line, Yokosuka Line, Gotemba Line, Minobu Line, Iida Line, Takeyoto Line, and Fukuchiyama Line. However, when JNR was divided and privatized, the “Basic Plan Concerning the Succession of Business, etc., of Japan National Railways, as well as Rights and Obligations” stipulated that the name for this line (excluding the Gotemba Line, etc.) would be “Tokaido Line.” Since then, both names have been used concurrently. For example, in documents issued by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism and in the ministry-supervised “Railway Almanac,” the name “Tokaido Line” is used, whereas in JNR’s official announcements of line names, the name “Tokaido Main Line” is used. Nevertheless, on the websites of the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism and each JR company, both names are used interchangeably.

In the Tokyo suburban area, for passenger guidance purposes, the term “Tokaido Line” refers to both medium-distance electric trains and limited express trains bound for Odawara and Atami. To distinguish these from the short-distance electric trains (commonly known as National Railways trains) that run concurrently between Tokyo Station and Ofuna Station, system names such as the Yamanote Line, Keihin-Tohoku Line, and Yokosuka Line are used.

Furthermore, after the division and privatization of the Japanese National Railways, JR West established route nicknames for its jurisdictional sections within the urban network known as the Keihanshin area. Specifically, the section of the Tokaido Main Line from Mihara Station to Kyoto Station was named the “Biwa Lake Line,” the section from Kyoto Station to Osaka Station was named the “JR Kyoto Line,” and the section from Osaka Station to Kobe Station was named the “JR Kobe Line.” In the Kansai region, it is common for users to refer to these routes by their nicknames, and mass media in the Kansai area, particularly television stations based in Osaka, also report on them using these route nicknames.

The fact that trains from Tennoji Station, the terminal station, operate directly on the Sanyo Main Line is referred to as the “Tokaido-Sanyo Main Line.” With the opening of the Ueno-Tokyo Line in 2015, direct services began from Tokyo Station, the starting point, to the Utsunomiya Line, Takasaki Line, and Joban Line sections of the Tohoku Main Line. As a result, the Tohoku Main Line, which had previously been connected only to the Keihin-Tohoku Line, Yamanote Line, and other electric lines up to Kanda on the Tokaido Main Line, became fully connected. Consequently, direct services now run between the Tohoku Main Line and the Sanyo Main Line, the major arteries of Honshu, at both the starting and terminal points.

In the JR East section, the area between Tokyo Station and Odawara Station includes multiple tracks (eight tracks between Tokyo Station and Shinagawa Station) on the Yamanote Line, Keihin-Tohoku Line, Yokosuka Line, and Tokaido Freight Line, among others. In the JR Tokai section, the area between Nagoya Station and Inazawa Station, and in the JR West section (including the Biwa Line, JR Kyoto Line, and JR Kobe Line), the area between Kusatsu Station and Kobe Station are also equipped with multiple tracks. The section between Kobe Station and Nishi-Akashi Station on the Sanyo Main Line, including the area from Kusatsu Station to Nishi-Akashi Station, is Japan's longest multiple-track section (120.9 km), and it is utilized to handle trains with different operating speeds and performance characteristics, such as the Shin-Kaisoku services.

Nao, because the Tokaido Shinkansen (managed by HaJR Tokai) was constructed as an additional line to the Ha Tokaido Main Line, from that perspective, if the same Shinkansen section between Shin-Osaka Station and Shin-Kobe Station (JR West Japan) is included within the Tokaido Main Line, and Shin-Kobe Station is treated as Kobe Station, then the entire Tokaido Main Line, excluding its branch lines, would become a double-double track line (and above). Before the opening of the Tohoku Shinkansen in 1982, the Shinkansen was treated as a completely separate additional line; however, according to the JR Line Name Announcement at that time, the section of the Tokaido Shinkansen between Shin-Osaka Station and Shin-Kobe Station was treated as an unnamed branch line of the Tokaido Main Line. On the other hand, in the basic business plan and the "Railway Yearbook" from that time, it was treated as a separate line.
章节.Meiji Period:
When the Meiji era began, the government had plans for a railway connecting Tokyo and Osaka. At that time, there were two proposals: one via the Tokaido route and another via the Nakasendo route. The direction had not yet been decided because, first, the busy Tokyo–Yokohama section was opened ahead of schedule as a branch line. On October 14, 1872 (Meiji 5, September 12 of the old calendar), the section between Shimbashi Station (present-day Shiodome Station) and Yokohama Station (present-day Sakuragicho Station) opened as Japan’s first railway. On September 15 of the following year, freight train operations also began. Meanwhile, in the Kansai region, after the provisional opening of the Osaka Station–Kobe Station section in 1874 (Meiji 7), commercial operations between Kyoto Station and Kobe Station began on February 5, 1877 (Meiji 10). In 1880 (Meiji 13), the line was extended via Ohsaka Pass to Otsu Station (near present-day Omi-Hama-Otsu Station), and a railway ferry service connecting Otsu Station and Nagahama Station via Lake Biwa was established by Taihukisen.

In August 1883 (Meiji 16), the government had already decided to construct the line between Tokyo and Takasaki (present-day Takasaki Line). Taking this into consideration, it was decided to construct the main railway line between Tokyo and Osaka via the Nakasendo Road (the Nakasendo Main Line). In the Chubu region, however, in order to transport materials for the construction of the Nakasendo Line, the section between Takeyama Station and Kiso River Station, which is now part of the Takeyama Line, opened in 1886 (Meiji 19). Again, in 1884 (Meiji 17), the section between Ogaki Station, Sekihara Station, and Nagahama Station opened as part of the Nakasendo Route. However, in July 1886, the government changed the planned route for the Tokyo-Osaka railway from via the Nakasendo to via the Tokaido, as it was anticipated that construction would be difficult and the construction period could be halved. Nevertheless, in order to actively utilize existing lines and reduce construction costs, the section between Nagoya and Kusatsu was laid along the Mino Road and the Nakasendo, which had been the Tokaido during the Edo period.

After this, a large-scale project was carried out all at once. In 1887 (Meiji 20), the sections between Kiso River Station and Kano Station (present-day Gifu Station) and Ogaki Station, between Yokohama Station and Kofutsu Station, and between Hamamatsu Station and Obu Station opened. The section between Takeyoto Station and Obu Station was converted into a branch line. In 1889 (Meiji 22), the section between Kofutsu Station and Hamamatsu Station (present-day Gotemba Line route) opened, and in July of the same year, the section between Sekihara Station, Yonehara Station, and Baba Station (present-day Zenisho Station) opened. Thus, 17 years and several months had passed since the opening of the Shinbashi Station–Yokohama Station section, and a 600.2 km railway link was established from Shinbashi Station to Kobe Station. At that time, one round-trip through service operated on the entire line, taking just over 20 hours. Although an official line name had not yet been established, the line was designated as the "Tokaido Line" in 1895 (Meiji 28). At that time, the route differed in the difficult-to-traverse areas of Izu, Hakone, Mount Ibuki, and Mount Ousaka.

Initially, from the post towns, opposition was carried out with slogans such as, “Customers will stop coming to the post town” and “The train will cause a fire.” As a result, because many routes were constructed in the suburbs due to the difficulty in acquiring land in the urban areas, it is also said that many stations were built at locations far from the post towns (the “railroad avoidance legend”). However, records in newspapers of the time and prefectural records, etc., show that each post town along the Tokaido actively campaigned to attract the railway; records of opposition movements are not found, so this view is also denied.

After the end of the First Sino-Japanese War in October 1895 (Meiji 28), direct services began from Kobe Station to the Sanyo Railway (currently the Sanyo Main Line). The following year, in 1896 (Meiji 29), express train services started between Shimbashi Station and Kobe Station (no express surcharge was required, and the travel time was reduced by about 4 hours to 17 hours and 22 minutes). In 1900 (Meiji 33), sleeping cars were added, and in 1901 (Meiji 34), dining cars were also added. In 1906 (Meiji 39), the fastest train was introduced, and by 1909 (Meiji 42), the journey time between Shimbashi Station and Kobe Station had been shortened to 12 hours and 50 minutes. In 1912 (Meiji 45), the final year of the Meiji era, the fastest train was changed to a Limited Express (Tokkyu) and operated between Shimbashi Station and Shimonoseki Station on the Sanyo Main Line.
章节.Taisho and Early Showa Periods:
On December 20, 1914 (Taisho 3), Niwa Tokyo Station Ga opened Shi, and the same station Ga became the starting point of the Tokaido Main Line Tta. At the same time, electric train service (currently the Keihin-Tohoku Line) between Tokyo Station and Takashima Station Ga began to run Saretei Ru.

During the Taisho period, in order to increase transport capacity on the Ninaruto route, it became necessary to change the route regarding the aforementioned difficult sections. As a result, new routes were constructed through the Ousaka Mountains (between Otsu Station and Kyoto Station), namely the New Ousaka Mountain Tunnel and the Higashiyama Tunnel, and by 1921 (Taisho 10), the current route was established. The travel time for express trains between Tokyo Station and Kobe Station was 11 hours and 45 minutes. Regarding the Izu and Hakone areas (between Kofutsu Station and Numazu Station), plans were made to construct a separate route, and by 1925 (Taisho 14), the section between Kofutsu Station and Atami Station was opened as the “Atami Line.” However, the opening of the Atami Station–Numazu Station section was delayed because the construction of the Tanna Tunnel proved extremely difficult. Meanwhile, around this time, electrification work on the railway line began from the Tokyo side, and by 1928 (Showa 3), the electrification of the Tokyo Station–Atami Station section was completed, leading to the start of operations using electric locomotives to replace steam locomotives.

In 1929 (Showa 4), the first limited express trains with affectionate names, "Fuji" and "Sakura," were introduced. The following year, in 1930 (Showa 5), the super express "Tsubame" appeared. In 1934 (Showa 9), the Tanna Tunnel opened, completing the current route between Kofu Station and Numazu Station. The old route was renamed the Gotemba Line. At the same time, the electrified section was extended to cover the area between Tokyo Station and Numazu Station, and the travel time for the "Tsubame" between Tokyo Station and Kobe Station became 8 hours and 37 minutes. Again, from that year onward, train services (local trains and express trains) began operating in the Keihan-Shin area. In July 1937 (Showa 12), the limited express trains increased to a schedule of 5 round trips per day, and this period is considered the golden age of the Tokaido Main Line before the war.

During the Second Sino-Japanese War and the start of the Pacific War, under the wartime system, freight trains were increased and lengthened to transport various supplies. In 1944 (Showa 19), based on the Outline of Emergency Measures for Decisive Battles, travel was significantly restricted. Then, on April 1 of the same year, with a timetable revision, all limited express trains were abolished, and express trains were also reduced. The attachment of sleeping cars, dining cars, etc., was also discontinued. Entering 1945 (Showa 20), stations, tracks, and rolling stock were destroyed by air raids and machine-gun strafing by Allied forces.

章节.Mid-Shōwa Period:
In 1945 (Showa 20), Japan was defeated in the war. During the subsequent period of chaos, there were shortages of both electricity and coal for operating steam locomotives. Furthermore, the introduction of dedicated vehicles for the Allied forces disrupted train schedules, leading to a time when limited express, express, first-class, and second-class trains ceased operations entirely. Due to a shortage of passenger cars, freight cars were also used for passenger transport.

In 1948 (Showa 23), express trains were finally reintroduced. After the establishment of Japanese National Railways as a public corporation in 1949 (Showa 24), the first postwar limited express train, the "Heiwa," began service (later renamed the "Tsubame"). Electrification also resumed its westward extension from Numazu Station. In 1950 (Showa 25), the limited express "Hato" was added to the "Tsubame," and the travel time, which had been extended during the war, was reduced back to prewar levels. In the Tokyo area, conventional passenger car trains were converted to electric multiple units, and the "Shonan Electric Train" service commenced.

In 1956 (Showa 31), the entire Tokaido Main Line was fully electrified. This enabled the limited express "Tsubame" and "Hato" to complete the Tokyo–Osaka journey in 7 hours and 30 minutes. In 1958 (Showa 33), sleeper trains (blue trains) using 20-series passenger cars began operation. Additionally, the first electric limited express train, the "Kodama," which utilized 151-series EMUs, started service, connecting Tokyo and Osaka in 6 hours and 50 minutes, and Tokyo and Kobe in 7 hours and 20 minutes. In 1960 (Showa 35), the "Tsubame" and "Hato" were also converted to electric multiple units, and parlor cars replaced the previous observation cars. Numerous other superior-class trains were also added to the schedule. Among freight trains, the high-speed container train "Takara" began operation in 1959 (Showa 34). Meanwhile, spurred by the period of high economic growth and the decision to host the Tokyo Olympics in 1964, plans for line expansions to increase transport capacity were proposed, leading to the decision to construct a separate line with standard gauge. Construction began in 1959 (Showa 34), and this line would eventually open as the Tokaido Shinkansen.

章节.Limited express trains:
Before the opening of the Tokaido Shinkansen in 1964, numerous superior trains (limited express, express, and semi-express) such as the “Tsubame,” “Hato,” and “Kodama” were operated, connecting various cities along the line. However, after the Tokaido Shinkansen opened, the Shinkansen took over the function of intercity transportation, and the number of superior trains on this line was reduced. The “Tokai,” which was the last remaining service to retain its classification from the JNR era as a semi-express, express, or limited express, was also discontinued in 2007. Currently, no daytime superior trains are scheduled to run through the entire line; the only superior trains operating within the line are the commuter limited expresses “Shonan” and “Bi-Express,” which were introduced after the establishment of JR. On the other hand, superior trains that pass through certain sections of this line to destinations such as the Izu Peninsula, Koshin region, Hida region of Gifu Prefecture, Hokuriku region, Kita-Kinki region, and San'in region, as well as areas along other lines, still exist today. Since the establishment of JR, they have also been utilized effectively for freight lines and other purposes.

Trains bound for the Nanki area can access the Narita International Airport and Kansai International Airport via the Limited Express Ga Ri.
From Mishima Station to Fuji Station, and from Shizuoka Station to Nagoya Station, no regular daytime limited express services are scheduled. On the other hand, from Numazu Station to Hamamatsu Station, and from Nagoya Station to Ogaki Station, Home Liner services (officially ordinary trains, not superior trains) operate under a boarding ticket system.

There are numerous overnight limited express and express trains that operate within the line, connect areas along this line with San'in, Shikoku, Kyushu, Hokuriku, and Tohoku regions, and use sleeping cars; these sleeping car trains are called the Blue Train. However, after the division and privatization of Japan National Railways and the establishment of JR, due to a decrease in passengers, various trains were discontinued or consolidated. The Blue Train, which had been running as a regular service on the Tokaido Main Line, disappeared in 2012 with the "Nihonkai" becoming a temporary train. Currently, the only remaining overnight train as a regular service is the Sunrise Express, which uses sleeping cars.

章节.Freight Train:
Freight train service between Shimbashi Station and Yokohama Station began on September 15, 1873, approximately one year after the stations opened. Since then, although the scale of operations was significantly reduced by the end of the JNR era, freight trains have continued to run on the Tokaido Main Line for about 140 years.

As of the March 2014 timetable revision, well then, between Tsurumi Station and Suita Freight Terminal Station, 35 to 40 round trips of regular container high-speed freight trains operate daily. Among these, one round trip connects Tokyo Freight Terminal Station and Anjigawaguchi Station on the Sakurajima Line using M250-series freight electric trains (Super Rail Cargo), covering the distance between the two stations in 6 hours and 12 minutes. Trains connecting the Tokyo metropolitan area with the Nagoya area and the Keihanshin area, as well as trains originating or terminating in Hokkaido, Tohoku, Sanyo, Kyushu, and other regions, also pass through this line. Additionally, about 10 round trips of trains that run directly through the Hokuriku Main Line and other Japan Sea longitudinal lines operate daily between Oohara Station and Inazawa Station, and between Kasadera Station and Mino-Akasaka Station. Due to the large number of such trains, during the late-night hours when few passenger trains run, up to six freight trains may operate per hour on this line. Furthermore, dedicated freight trains for transporting limestone and other cargo operate between Oofu Station and Inazawa Station, and between Kasadera Station and Mino-Akasaka Station. On the Tokaido Main Line, regular freight trains depart from and arrive at Tokyo Freight Terminal Station, Kawasaki Freight Station, Yokohama Hazawa Station, Sagami Freight Station, Numazu Station, Fuji Station, Shizuoka Freight Station, Nishihama-matsu Station, Inazawa Station, Gifu Freight Terminal Station, Kyoto Freight Station, Suita Freight Terminal Station, and Osaka Freight Terminal Station (as of the March 15, 2014 timetable revision). Additionally, Kawasaki Freight Station, Kasadera Station, and Mino-Akasaka Station are connected to dedicated freight lines.
Furthermore, between Odawara Station and beyond in the Tokyo metropolitan area, and between Ibaraki Station and Amagasaki Station near Osaka, freight trains run on separate dedicated tracks from passenger trains (freight-passenger separation). Specifically, between Higashi-Totsuka Station and beyond, and between Shin-Osaka Station and Amagasaki Station, the running routes also differ from those of passenger trains. Additionally, between Nagoya Station and Inazawa Station (the Upper Line extends to Owari-Ichinomiya Station), a dedicated freight line known as the “Inazawa Line” runs in parallel.
章节.School Trip Trains: From 1959, school excursion trains bearing names such as "Hinode," "Kibō," and "Komadori" were operated using dedicated trainsets like the 155 series. These reached their peak around 1965, but school excursion transport eventually shifted to the Shinkansen, and school excursion trains on conventional lines had disappeared by 1973.
章节.Rolling Stock:
This section lists the main types of rolling stock that have been used on this line, divided into three categories: trains for regular services, trains for limited express services, and locomotives.

Regarding passenger trains, from the line's opening until some time after electrification was completed, most services consisted of passenger car trains hauled by locomotives (steam locomotives before electrification, and electric locomotives afterward). After the introduction of medium-distance electric train services from the Tokyo end in 1950 (Showa 25), the electrification of passenger car trains progressed, and by October 1968 (Showa 43), all services except those directly connecting to other lines had been converted to electric train operation. Electric trains operating on this line, which uses DC electrification, are generally DC-only models. For services directly connecting to AC-electrified lines such as the Joban Line and Hokuriku Main Line, AC/DC multiple units are used, while for services directly connecting to non-electrified lines, diesel multiple units (DMUs) are employed. Freight trains, with the exception of a single round trip per day of the electric "Super Rail Cargo" service, are hauled by locomotives.

This section omits freight cars, service vehicles, as well as the mail and baggage cars used during the Japan National Railways era. For detailed information on operating sections, vehicle specifications, and other details, please refer to the articles on the specific vehicles or the region-specific articles mentioned at the beginning of this article.

November 28: Double-tracking between Noto River Station and Hachiman Station.
December 1: Double-tracking between Kase Station and Noto River Station.
December 5: Double-tracking between Yonehara Station and Kase Station.
December 28: Double-tracking between Seki Hara Station and Nagaoka Station.
1902 (Meiji 35)
January 1: Opening of Ni Konoya Seki Station on the Otsu Line.
February 10: Double-tracking between Tarui Station and Seki Hara Station.
April 15: Opening of Ninomiya Station.
June 16: Double-tracking between Nozu Station and Kusatsu Station. Abolition of Nozu River Signal Post.
September 1: Double-tracking between Gamagori Station and Okazaki Station.
November 1: Double-tracking between Nagaoka Station and Yonehara Station. Renaming of the section between Shinbashi Station and Kobe Station; extension of the same section by 8C ≒ 0.16 km. Separation of the section between Yonehara Station, Tsuruga Station, and Kanazaki Station as the Hokuriku Line.

November 12: The unit of operating distance was changed to miles and feet (between Shimbashi Station and Kobe Station, 375M17C → 375.2M; between Kanagawa Station and Yokohama Station, 1M55C → 1.7M; between Hattori Station and Yokohama Station, 2M38C → 2.5M).
December 21: The Ishibe Signal Box was opened between Shizuoka Station and Yaizu Station. The section between Shizuoka Station and Ishibe Signal Box was doubled.
1903 (Meiji 36)
January 20: The Kawakami Signal Box was opened between Hattori Station and Totsuka Station, and the Ashigara Signal Box was opened between Oyama Station and Gotemba Station.
April 1: Ishiyama Station opened.
July 6: The section between Washizu Station and Toyohashi Station was doubled.
December 7: The section between Kanaya Station and Horiuchi Station was doubled.
December 20: The Nagara Signal Box was opened between Gifu Station and Hodozumi Station. The section between Gifu Station and Nagara Signal Box was doubled.
1904 (Meiji 37)
February 1: The Nada Signal Box (currently Higashi-Nada Signal Point) was opened between Sumiyoshi Station and Miya Station.
February 8: The section between Hamamatsu Station and Maisaka Station was doubled.
April 11: Kamata Station opened.
May 1: The Nori Signal Box was opened between Osaka Station and Kanzaki Station.
August 5: The section between Maisaka Station and Washizu Station was doubled. Inazawa Station opened.
1905 (Meiji 38)

February 1: Ni-Koyasu Signal Station opened between Tsurumi Station and Higashi-Kanagawa Station.
February 20: The section between Tenryugawa Station and Hamamatsu Station was doubled.
April 5: The section between Hori-no-uchi Station and Kakegawa Station was doubled.
1906 (Meiji 39)
April: Ni-Ashitani Signal Station opened between Gamagori Station and Okazaki Station.
April 16: Kiyosu Station (first) was relocated and renamed to Biwa-jima Station. Kiyosu Signal Station was opened at the site of the former station.
July 1: The freight branch line (Hiratsuka Branch Line) starting from Hiratsuka Station was opened as a non-revenue line. The name of the terminal station is unknown (also known as Hiratsuka Freight Handling Point).
July 11: Benten-jima Station (first) opened.
August 1: Hodzumi Station opened.
September 11: Benten-jima Station (first) was closed.
1907 (Meiji 40)
March 1: The section between Kiyosu Signal Station and Kiso-gawa Station was doubled.
March 15: Tomoda Signal Station was opened between Kanaya Station and Hori-no-uchi Station, and Tani-ga Signal Station was opened between Yamakita Station and Koyama Station.
March 27: The section between Nagoya Station and Biwa-jima Station was doubled.
April 8: The section between Biwa-jima Station and Kiyosu Signal Station was doubled.
April 9: Kiyomiji Temporary Stop was opened between Kotsu Station and Ejiri Station. A special train for Empress Shoken's visit to Kiyomiji Temple stopped there.

April 10: Kiyomidera Temporary Stop Ga abolished.
April 19: Kiyosu Signal Post Ga abolished.
April 20: The section between Yaizu Station and Shimada Station Ga becomes double-tracked.
June 13: The section between Obu Station and Ohtaka Station Ga becomes double-tracked.
June 15: Bentenjima Temporary Station Ga opens.
August 20: The freight branch line (Kobe Port Line) section between Nada Liaison Post and Onohama Freight Handling Post (2.0M≒3.22 km) opens. Nada Signal Post o renamed to Nada Liaison Post Ni. Onohama Freight Handling Post (Nochino Onohama Station→Kobe Port Station) Ga opens.
September 26: The section between Ohtaka Station and Atsuta Station Ga becomes double-tracked.
November 1: The freight branch line section between Numazu Station and Jyamatsu Station (2.0M) and the Hiratsuka Branch Line (1.0M≒1.61 km) Ga officially open. (Freight) Jyamatsu Station (later no Numazu Port Station) Ga officially opens. The section between Kanagawa Station and Yokohama Station bi is integrated with the section between Hekiyatani Station and Yokohama Station Shi, and the route between Kanagawa Station and Yokohama Station - Hekiyatani Station Ni is changed.
December 20: The section between Kakegawa Station and Fukuroi Station Ga becomes double-tracked.
1908 (Meiji 41) goro: Onohama Freight Handling Post o renamed to Onohama Station Ni.
1908 (Meiji 41)
February 2: The section between Kariya Station and Obu Station Ga becomes double-tracked.

February 10: Nishinomiya Station - Sumiyoshi Station section: Nishinomiya Ebisu Temporary Stop (first generation) opened. Between Kanzaki Station and Nishinomiya Station, the first Mukogawa Temporary Signal Box was established; between Nishinomiya Station and Sumiyoshi Station, the first Ashiya Temporary Signal Box was established. Additional trains were operated to accommodate the Nishinomiya Grand Shrine Festival.
February 12: Nishinomiya Ebisu Temporary Stop (first generation), Mukogawa Temporary Signal Box (first generation), and Ashiya Temporary Signal Box (first generation) were all discontinued.
February 22: Nishinomiya Station - Sumiyoshi Station section: Okamoto Temporary Stop (first generation) opened, for passenger transport to Okamoto Plum Blossom Park.
March 16: Okamoto Temporary Stop (first generation) was discontinued.
March 28: The sections between Fukuroi Station and Chuuizumi Station, and between Anjo Station and Karigaya Station, were doubled.
April 29: The section between Hodzumi Station and Ogaki Station was doubled.
June 2: The section between Toyohashi Station and Miyu Station was doubled.
June 29: The section between Miyu Station and Gamagori Station was doubled.
July 29: The section between Okazaki Station and Anjo Station was doubled.
September 11: Ashiya Signal Box was converted into a station, and Koda Station opened.
September 23: Higashikannai Station opened.
October 26: Between Chuuizumi Station and Tenryugawa Station, the Tenryugawa East Bank Signal Box was established on the Tenryugawa River's east bank.
November 5: The section between Chuuizumi Station and Tenryugawa Signal Box was doubled.

November 16: The Ni-Takabata Provisional Signal Station between Suita Station and Osaka Station, the Ni-Mukogawa Provisional Signal Station (2nd generation) between Kanzaki Station and Nishi-no-Miya Station, and the Ni-Ashiya Provisional Signal Station (2nd generation) between Nishi-no-Miya Station and Sumiyoshi Station are opened. The Ni-Takabata Provisional Signal Station, Ni-Mukogawa Provisional Signal Station (2nd generation), and Ni-Ashiya Provisional Signal Station (2nd generation) are opened to accommodate increased train services for the naval review held at Kobe Port.
November 19: The Takabata Provisional Signal Station, Mukogawa Provisional Signal Station (2nd generation), and Ashiya Provisional Signal Station (2nd generation) are discontinued.
1909 (Meiji 42)
February 8: The Okamoto Provisional Stop (2nd generation) opens.
April 21: Fuji Station opens.
June 11: The Kiso Bridge Signal Station is opened between Kiso River Station and Gifu Station. The Nagara Signal Station is discontinued.
June 15: The section between Kiso Bridge Signal Station and Gifu Station, and the section between Nagara Signal Station and Hozumi Station are doubled.
October 12: The names of the national railway lines are established. The section between Shinbashi Station and Kobe Station, the branch line between Kanagawa Station, Yokohama Station, and Tokiwa Valley Station, the freight branch line between Numazu Station and Jyamatsu Station, and the section between Nada Connecting Point and Onohama Station are all designated as the Tokaido Main Line. The section between Oi Connecting Point and Osaki Station is designated as the Yamanote Line Freight Branch, the section between Ofuna Station and Yokosuka Station as the Yokosuka Line, the section between Obu Station and Takeyoto Station as the Takeyoto Line, and the section between Baba Station and Otsu Station as the Otsu Line.

November 1: Yōmune Station Ga opens. The Ishibe Signal Box between Yōmune Station and Yaizu Station Ga is abolished.
November 24: The Ishibe Provisional Signal Box Ni is opened between Yōmune Station and Yaizu Station.
December 16: The electric railway line (0.7M≒1.13 km) Ga opens between Hamamatsuchō Station and Karasumori Station. The section between Hamamatsuchō Station and Shinagawa Station Ga becomes quadruple-track (with the laying of an electric railway line). Tamachi Station, Hamamatsuchō Station, and Karasumori Station (currently Shimbashi Station) Ga open. The Shuto Loop Line to Shiteno Yamanote Line no begins.
December 21: The Ebisu Provisional Stop (second generation) opens Ni between Nishinomiya Station and Sumiyoshi Station (the first generation served the same purpose). The Mukogawa Provisional Signal Box (third generation) o is opened Ni between Kanzaki Station and Nishi-no-Miya Station, and the Ashiya Provisional Signal Box (third generation) o is opened Ni between Nishi-no-Miya Station and Sumiyoshi Station (the abolition dates for both are unknown).
1910 (Meiji 43)
February 21: The Ibarakigawa Provisional Signal Box (first generation) o is opened Ni between Takatsuki Station and Ibaraki Station.
March 6: The section between Fujikawa Signal Box and Iwabuchi Station Ga is doubled.
March 15: The Fujikawa Signal Box Ga is abolished.

March 29: Between Kyoto Station and Mukōmach Station, Ni Kichijōin Signal Box o; between Mukōmach Station and Yamazaki Station, Ni Kanzoku Signal Box o; between Yamazaki Station and Takatsuki Station, Ni Kajihara Signal Box o; between Takatsuki Station and Ibaraki Station, Ni Tomita Signal Box o; between Ibaraki Station and Suita Station, Ni Tsuboi Signal Box o; between Suita Station and Osaka Station, Ni Yamaguchi Signal Box o; between Kanzaki Station and Nishinomiya Station, Ni Mizuno Signal Box o; between Nishinomiya Station and Sumiyoshi Station, Ni Uchide Signal Box o opened.
April 2: Ibarakigawa Provisional Signal Box (first generation) Ga discontinued.
June 25: The electric line (0.7M) between Karasumori Station and Yurakucho Station Ga extended and opened. Yurakucho Station Ga opened.
August 24: Between Kahara Station and Kōtsu Station, Ni Dōtunnel Provisional Signal Box (first generation) o opened (discontinuation date unknown).
September 15: The electric line (0.7M) between Yurakucho Station and Kofu Bridge Station Ga extended and opened. Kofu Bridge Station (provisional station of Tokyo Station) Ga opened.
October 1: Nada Liaison Office o changed to a station, and (freight) Nada Station (first generation) Ga opened.
October 6: Between Yōmune Station and Yaizu Station, Ni Isohama Provisional Signal Box o opened.
November 1: The section between Isohama Provisional Signal Box and Yaizu Station Ga double-tracked.
November 5: Between Kyoto Station and Mukōmach Station, Ni Umekōji Provisional Signal Box and Katsuragawa Signal Box o opened. Kichijōin Signal Box Ga discontinued.
December 8: Ishibe Provisional Signal Box discontinued.

1911 (Meiji 44)
February 25: Ume-no-Koji Provisional Signal Station o Provisional Station toshi Ume-no-Koji Provisional Station opens. A provisional station exclusively for groups of worshippers attending the grand Buddhist ceremony at Nishi Hongan-ji and Chion-in.
March 9: Isohama Provisional Signal Station Ga is abolished. Between Kahara Station and Kotsu Station, the second Uodo Tunnel Provisional Signal Station is opened (date of abolition unknown).
March 10: The section between Yomune Station and Isohama Provisional Signal Station Ga is doubled.
March 31: Between Hamamatsu Station and Masaka Station, the Takatsuka Signal Station is opened.
April 10: Between Ejiri Station and Shizuoka Station, the Kusanagi Signal Station is opened.
May 1: The freight branch line (Nagoya Port Line) between Nagoya Station and Nagoya Port Station (5.0M ≒ 8.05 km) Ga opens. (Freight) Nagoya Port Station opens. Between Hekitani Station and Totsuka Station, the Gongen Signal Station is opened; between Totsuka Station and Ofuna Station, the Kubo Signal Station is opened; between Kofutsu Station and Matsuda Station, the Shimosoga Signal Station is opened; between Gotemba Station and Sano Station, the Fujioka Signal Station and Iwanami Signal Station are opened. Kamiyama Signal Station Ga is abolished.
May 5: Ume-no-Koji Provisional Station toshi is changed to a liaison office, and Ume-no-Koji Liaison Office opens.
June 28: Passenger service begins on the Nagoya Port Line between Nagoya Station and Nagoya Port Station.
September 1: Yokohama Port Freight Handling Office is opened within the Yokohama Station premises.
1912 (Meiji 45)

April 16: Moroyama Station opens.
April 17: The Nii-Ibarakigawa Provisional Signal Station (second generation) opens between Takatsuki Station and Ibaraki Station (date of closure unknown).
June 15: The Okawagawa Signal Station opens between Kusatsu Station and Ishiyama Station.
July 1: Koyama Station is renamed Suruga Station.
July 18: Iwanami Signal Station is renamed Iwanami Signal Station.
July 27: The section between Shimada Station and Kanaya Station is doubled.
1913 (Taisho 2)
February 1: The section between Kiso River Station and Kiso Bridge Signal Station is doubled. Kiso Bridge Signal Station is closed.
March 1: The Otsu Line (1.3M) is incorporated as a freight branch line. The Iba Station and Konya-zeki Station on this line are closed. The Shirasuga Signal Station opens between Washizu Station and Futagawa Station.
March 15: The Tsujido Signal Station opens between Fujisawa Station and Chigasaki Station.
April 5: The Otsuka Signal Station opens between Otani Station and Yamashina Station.
June 1: Baba Station is renamed Otsu Station (second generation), and the original Otsu Station is renamed Hamadaotsu Station.
June 2: The Takashima Freight Handling Yard is opened within Yokohama Station premises.
June 21: The Umekoji Linkage Office is changed to a station, and Umekoji Station opens.
August 1: The Uchide Signal Station is changed to a station, and Ashiya Station opens. The Tenryugawa Bridge is doubled, completing the doubling of the entire line.

October 25: Ni Miyahara Signal Station opened between Suita Station and Osaka Station. Yamaguchi Signal Station closed.
November 27: Ni Haranogawa Provisional Signal Station opened between Fukuroi Station and Nakaizumi Station, for the repair of Haranogawa Bridge.
1914 (Taisho 3)
March 31: Haranogawa Provisional Signal Station closed.
April 25: Azuchi Station opened.
September 13: Ni Takenoshita Provisional Signal Station opened between Suruga Station and Gotemba Station.
October 24: Ni Nagara River Provisional Signal Station (first) opened between Gifu Station and Hozumi Station.
December 1: Nagaoka Station renamed to Omi-Nagaoka Station.
December 20: Between Tokyo Station and the section from Kanagawa Station to Yokohama Station, Takashimacho Station and Oi Liaison Point were changed to stations, and Oi-machi Station opened. Shimbashi Station (first) was renamed to Shiodome Station, and Karasumori Station was renamed to Shimbashi Station (second).

Kurefukubashi Station closed. Between Kurefukubashi Station and Tokyo Station (0.2M ≒ 0.32 km) o Abolished; the branch line between Tokyo Station and Hamamatsuchō Station (1.9M) o Incorporated into the main line Ni; the section between Hamamatsuchō Station and Shinagawa Station (2.4M) Mo Listed under the main line Ni. Replaced by passenger train operations between Shimbashi Station and Yokohama Station; electric train operations (Keihin Electric Railway, now the Keihin-Tōhoku Line) commenced between Tokyo Station and Takashimachō Station; at the same time, the section between Shinagawa Station and Yokohama Station was quadruplicated. Passenger services between Shiodome Station and Shinagawa Station (3.1M) abolished.
December 24: Izusarako Signal Box opened on the electric line between Tamachō Station and Shinagawa Station.
1915 (Taishō 4)
January 10: Niimachō Station opened.
February 15: Sengawa Provisional Signal Box opened between Yamakita Station and Tanihama Signal Box; Aizawa Provisional Signal Box opened between Tanihama Signal Box and Suruga Station.
February 24: Ebisu Provisional Stop (2nd) and Okamoto Provisional Stop (2nd) abolished. Passenger services on the Nagoya Port Line between Nagoya Station and Nagoya Port Station abolished.
April 19: Nagarakawa Provisional Signal Box (1st) abolished.
May 10: Tenryūbashi Signal Box abolished.
June 20: Sengawa Provisional Signal Box and Aizawa Provisional Signal Box abolished.
July 10: Matsuzawa Provisional Signal Box opened between Suruga Station and Gotemba Station.

July 15: Sano Station and Susono Station were renamed.
August 15: The route between Kanagawa Station and Hokegaya Station was changed (no change in distance). On the new line, Yokohama Station (the second one, currently near Takashimacho Station on the Yokohama Municipal Subway Line 3) opened. Takashimacho Station and Hirinuma Station on the old line were closed. Yokohama Station (the first one) was renamed Sakuragicho Station. The starting point of the Sakuragicho Station branch line was changed from Kanagawa Station to Yokohama Station (a shortening of 0.7 miles ≈ 1.13 km). The section between Sakuragicho Station and Hokegaya Station (2.5 miles ≈ 4.02 km) was closed.
At this point, the junction between the main line and the Sakuragicho Station branch line was at Kanagawa Station, and the two lines crossed at grade at Yokohama Station. Again, Takashimacho Station was located near Yokohama Station's Keihin Electric Railway home platform.
August 30: Matsuzawa Provisional Signal Station and Takenoshita Provisional Signal Station were closed.
December 25: The second Nagara River Provisional Siding was opened between Gifu Station and Hodozumi Station.
December 30: The freight branch line (Takashima Line) section between Hokegaya Station and Higashi-Yokohama Station (3.3 miles ≈ 5.31 km) opened. Higashi-Yokohama Station opened. The Takashima Freight Handling Area was separated from Sakuragicho Station, and Takashima Station (freight) opened. The branch line section between Yokohama Station and Sakuragicho Station was electrified, and freight operations were discontinued. The operating section of the Keihin Electric Railway was extended to Sakuragicho Station.

1916 (Taisho 5)
January 1: Ichinomiya Station was renamed to Owari-Ichinomiya Station.
March 3: The second Nagara River Provisional Signal Station was abolished.
April 6: The Takamiya River Provisional Signal Station was opened between Hikone Station and Kawase Station (date of abolition unknown).
April 15: Yui Station opened.
April 16: The freight branch line of the Yamanote Line between Osaki Station and Oimachi Station was abolished.
May 16: The first Ota River Provisional Siding was opened between Fukuroi Station and Nakaizumi Station (date of abolition unknown).
July 10: The freight branch line (Shimizu Port Line) between Ejiri Station and Shimizu Port Station (1.0 mi ≈ 1.61 km) opened. *(Freight) Shimizu Port Station opened.
August 28: The Sakawa Provisional Signal Station was opened.
September 1: Bentenjima Provisional Halt was upgraded to Bentenjima Station.
November 6: The Sakawa Provisional Signal Station was abolished.
December 1: Tsujido Signal Station was upgraded to Tsujido Station.
December 8: The Nagoya Port Line between Yahata Connecting Point and Shiratori Station (1.1 mi ≈ 1.77 km) opened. (Freight) Shiratori Station opened. Yahata Connecting Point was established as the junction point between the Nagoya Port direction and the Shiratori direction.
December 13: The second Ota River Provisional Siding was opened between Fukuroi Station and Nakaizumi Station (date of abolition unknown).
1917 (Taisho 6)

January 15: Onohama Station premises began handling cargo, and the Kobe Port Cargo Handling Office was established.
February 12: The Kiso Bridge Provisional Signal Station (first generation) was established between Kiso River Station and Gifu Station (date of closure unknown).
June 17: The Takashima Line sections between Tsurumi Station and Takashima Station (4.1 miles ≒ 6.66 km) and between Higashi-Kanagawa Station and Takashima Station (1.4 miles ≒ 2.25 km) opened. Ie Signal Station and Kaiganagawa Signal Handling Office were established.
October 9: The Numakawa Provisional Signal Station was established between Suzukawa Station and Fuji Station (date of closure unknown).
December 1: Nada Station (second generation) opened. The original (cargo) Nada Station was renamed (cargo) Higashi-Nada Station.
1918 (Taisho 7)
January 20: The Setogawa Provisional Signal Station was established between Yomune Station and Yaizu Station.
February 16: Isazaki Signal Station was closed.
April 1: Construction of the Tanna Tunnel began.
May 1: The Kawasaki Station–Hama-Kawasaki Station freight branch line (2.7 miles ≒ 4.35 km) opened. (Cargo) Hama-Kawasaki Station opened.
May 15: The Uta-shima Provisional Signal Station was established between Osaka Station and Kanzaki Station.
June 1: Shinohara Signal Station was established.

August 1: The freight branch line (Hokuhoku Freight Line) between Suita Station, Miyahara Connecting Yard, Miyahara Shunting Yard, Utaajima Connecting Yard, and Kanzaki Station (6.8M ≒ 10.94 km) opens. Miyahara Shunting Yard is established. Miyahara Signal Box is renamed Miyahara Connecting Yard, and Utaajima Provisional Signal Box is renamed Utaajima Connecting Yard.
August 25: Setogawa Provisional Signal Box is closed.
September 10: The freight branch line between Atsuta Station, Furuto Connecting Yard, and Chikusa Station (3.0M ≒ 4.83 km), and between Umekoji Station and Tanbaguchi Station (1.8M ≒ 2.90 km) opens.
1919 (Taisho 8)
February 25: Kiso Bridge Provisional Signal Box (second generation) is established between Kiso River Station and Gifu Station (date of closure unknown).
March 11: Hachiman Station is renamed Omi-Hachiman Station.
April 25: Arao Connecting Yard is established.
August 1: The branch line (Mino-Akasaka Line) between Ogaki Station, Arao Connecting Yard, and Mino-Akasaka Station (3.1M ≒ 4.99 km) opens (the section between Ogaki Station and Arao Connecting Yard is a shared section with the Ha line). Mino-Akasaka Station opens.
November 25: Teraura Signal Box is established between Kei Station and Yonehara Station.
1920 (Taisho 9)
July 1: Inaeda Station opens.

July 23: The Takashima Line extended and opened between Higashi-Yokohama Station and Yokohama-Port Station (1.6 mi ≈ 2.57 km). Yokohama-Port Station opened after being separated from Sakuragicho Station's Yokohama-Port Freight Handling Area. Passenger service began on the new line between Tsurumi Station and Higashi-Yokohama Station.
November 15: Noda Signal Box opened between Anjo Station and Karigaya Station.
December 15: Rozu Bridge Signal Box opened between Atsuta Station and Nagoya Station.
1921 (Taisho 10)
April 20: Shinohara Signal Box was converted into a station, and Shinohara Station opened.
May 1: Gonngen Signal Box, Kawakami Signal Box, and Kubo Signal Box were closed.
July 20: Katsuragawa Signal Box, Kanzoku Signal Box, Kajihara Signal Box, Tomita Signal Box, Tsuboi Signal Box, and Mizuno Signal Box were closed.
August 1: The New Ohsakayama Tunnel was completed, and the current line between Baba Station and Kyoto Station (7.2 mi ≈ 11.59 km) opened as a double-track line. The old line between Baba Station, Otani Station, and Inari Station (8.3 mi ≈ 13.36 km) was closed. The section between Inari Station and Kyoto Station (1.8 mi ≈ 2.90 km) was incorporated into the Nara Line. Otani Station, Otsuka Signal Box, and the first Yamashina Station were closed. The second Yamashina Station and the third Otsu Station opened. The second Otsu Station was renamed Baba Station.
1922 (Taisho 11)

February 1: Koyasu Signal Box was abolished.
February 18: Numa-iri Provisional Signal Box was opened between Kayanozaki Station and Hiratsuka Station (date of abolition unknown).
April 1: Signal boxes and liaison offices were changed to signal stations, and provisional signal boxes were changed to provisional signal stations.
May 15: Shimosoga Signal Station was changed to a station, and Shimosoga Station was opened.
1923 (Taisho 12)
Date unknown: Nozato Signal Station was abolished.
June 1: Suita Shunting Yard was opened.
July 1: Aoshima Signal Station was opened between Fujieda Station and Shimada Station, Umebashi Signal Station between Kakegawa Station and Fukuroi Station, Otsuka Signal Station between Miyu Station and Gamagori Station, and Fukamizu Signal Station between Gamagori Station and Koda Station.
September 1: The Great Kanto Earthquake occurred. The Yokohama Station building was burned down, and at Negofurukawa Station, a train was pushed by a landslide and fell, among other major damages. The section between Tokyo Station and Gotemba Station, among others, became impassable. Services were gradually restored and fully resumed on October 28.
1924 (Taisho 13)
April 1: The Hiratsuka Branch Line (1.0 mi ≈ 1.61 km) was abolished.
July 25: Setsumi Tomida Station was opened.

August 3: The Sanyo Main Line's Onohama Station - Kobe Port Station section (1.0M) is extended and opened. Onohama Station is separated from the Kobe Port Freight Handling Area, and Kobe Port Station (Kouminatoeki) is opened. Passenger service begins on the new line between Tonan Station and Onohama Station.
October 1: The Kaishinagawa Signal Handling Area on the Takashima Line is changed to Chiwaka Signal Yard.
1925 (Taisho 14)
January 16: The section between Nagoya Station and Inazawa Station is triple-tracked (Inazawa Line constructed).
February 16: Oogawagawa Signal Yard is abolished.
March 10: The freight branch line between Miyahara Signal Yard and Utaishima Signal Yard is double-tracked.
October 15: Kamioyodo Provisional Signal Yard is opened between Suita Station and Osaka Station. The section between Suita Station and Kamioyodo Provisional Signal Yard is quadruple-tracked.
December 13: The section between Yokohama Station and Kofutsu Station is electrified.
1926 (Taisho 15)
February 24: Tsuribashi Signal Yard is abolished.
April 3: Kusanagi Signal Yard is changed to a station, and Kusanagi Station is opened.
July 3: Sodeji Provisional Halt is opened between Kotsu Station and Ejiri Station.
July 8: Shiba Provisional Signal Yard is opened between Tamachi Station and Shinagawa Station on the Keihin Electric Line (abolition date unknown; previously located at the same site as Izarashiko Signal Post).
November 10: Setagawa Provisional Signal Yard is opened between Kusatsu Station and Ishiyama Station (abolition date unknown).

November 15: Quadruple-tracking between Uta-shima Signal Station and Higashi-nada Station. Uta-shima Signal Station (Ga) closed.
1927 (Showa 2)
February 12: Opening of the first Yui Station - Kotsu Station Ni-do Provisional Signal Station (Ga) (closure date unknown).
February 26: Noda Signal Station (Ga) closed.
August 19: Triple-tracking between Ofuna Station and Fujisawa Station (Ga).
September 2: Tera-kura Signal Station (Ga) closed.
September 26: Quadruple-tracking between Ofuna Station and Fujisawa Station (Ga).
October 18: Triple-tracking between Fujisawa Station and Kaya-ke-zaki Station (Ga).
November 8: Quadruple-tracking between Fujisawa Station and Tsujido Station (Ga).
1928 (Showa 3)
January 19: Extension and opening of Nagoya Port Line between Nagoya Port Station and Horikawaguchi Station (1.2M ≒ 1.93 km) (Ga). (Freight) Horikawaguchi Station (Ga) opened.
February 12: Otsuka Signal Station and Fukamizo Signal Station (Ga) closed.
March 20: Quadruple-tracking between Tsujido Station and Hiratsuka Station (Ga).
March 31: Quadruple-tracking between Hoke-dani Station and Ofuna Station (Ga).
June 2: Shirasuga Signal Station (Ga) closed.

October 15: Moved to the current location of Yokohama Station Ga, route changed between Kanagawa Station and Hattori Station (new line Ha used the old line track of Hirinuma Station noTta, no KairoNone). Kanagawa Station closed. At this point well then, because Keihin Line home had opened at Yokohama Station Ni, a temporary home was set up in front of the east exit of the former Keihin Line Yokohama Station, and the old Yokohama Station Keihin Line home remained as the Takashima-guchi boarding area.
December 1: (Freight) Umeda Station and (Freight) Minato-gawa Station opened.
December 7: The freight branch line between Shiodome Station and Shinagawa Station was electrified.
1929 (Showa 4)
January 24: The section between Ibaraki Station and Suita Station was quadruple-tracked.
March 15: Senri Signal Station was opened between Suita Station and Osaka Station.
April 9: Rosubashi Temporary Signal Station was opened between Atsuta Station and Nagoya Station.

章节.Vehicles for Local Trains: During the Japan National Railways (JNR) era, the trains used for local services (including rapid services) on this line were all-purpose models such as the 80 series, featuring two doors per side with cross seats, and the 113 series, with three doors per side and semi-cross seats. However, starting in the 1980s, in the highly competitive Keihan-Shin and Nagoya areas, the 117 series, equipped with comfortable two-door-per-side convertible cross seats, was introduced for rapid services. This marked the beginning of deploying vehicles tailored to local conditions. After the privatization and division of JNR, this trend accelerated, with each of the three passenger companies introducing and operating vehicles with their own unique specifications. In the Tokyo metropolitan area of JR East, where rush-hour congestion is severe, the focus has been on alleviating crowding. This has been achieved by increasing the number of longitudinal seats and introducing double-decker cars to boost capacity. Newer series such as the E217 series have also adopted four doors per side, similar to commuter trains, to reduce boarding and alighting times. In the Shizuoka area of JR Central, which primarily handles short-distance transport, vehicles introduced after privatization have also centered on longitudinal seating. In contrast, in the Nagoya area of JR Central and the Keihan-Shin area of JR West, vehicles inheriting the convertible cross seats of the 117 series, but with three doors per side like the 113 series, have become the mainstay.

This section opened as the first step toward constructing a route via Odawara (Hayakawa-guchi) Station and then via Atami, instead of going through Gotemba due to steep gradients, designating it as part of the Tokaido Main Line. Concurrently, the Odawara Electric Railway Line, a competing streetcar line, was discontinued. For more information on the railway situation in this area, see also "Odoriko."

章节.JR Central:
The conventional trains (including rapid services) of JR Central use suburban-type cars with three doors on each side. While the cars operated in the Shizuoka area (between Atami Station and Hamamatsu Station) and the Nagoya area (between Toyohashi Station and Yorigahara Station) are generally separate, cars from both areas operate between Hamamatsu Station and Toyohashi Station. Additionally, cars intended for the Nagoya area are also used on sections such as between Kakegawa Station and Hamamatsu Station. The Shizuoka-area cars feature longitudinal seating and are coupled in units of two or three cars, while the Nagoya-area cars have reversible cross seats and are typically formed into trainsets of four, six, or eight cars.
